articles.title: Societal Determinism: How do Mothers have an Influence on a Child's IQ?
articles.contents:
By: Akmal G on November 4th, 2025
For one of my first works while learning from the University of Essex, I created a visualization that shows how a mother’s education, IQ and work status combined to influence children’ test scores. The visualization revealed a number of patterns of advantages and disadvantages across different family backgrounds.
The kidiq data stems from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth and is used in Gelman and Hill (2007). The data set contains 434 observations measured on five variables, and is obtained from https: //github.com/jknowles/BDAexampleR.data
I used the packages tidyverse, stringr, readr, ggplot2 and curl.


knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(curl)


My approach was to create categories that combine mother’s education and work status. Then, I processed child outcomes vary across these combined categories.


# Download and mutate data
kidiq.raw <- read_csv("kidiq-2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
kidiq <- kidiq.raw %>%
mutate(
  
# Create work status labels
work_status = case_when(
mom_work == 1 ~ "Not working",
mom_work == 2 ~ "Part-time",
mom_work == 3 ~ "Full-time",
mom_work == 4 ~ "Full-time+"
),
# Create highschool diploma success groups
highschool_diploma = case_when(
mom_hs == 0 ~ "High School Diploma",
mom_hs == 1 ~ "No High School Diploma",
),
# Create combined advantage categories
family_advantage = case_when(
mom_hs == 0 & mom_work <= 2 ~ "Low",
mom_hs == 0 & mom_work > 2 ~ "Mixed",
mom_hs == 1 & mom_work <= 2 ~ "Mixed",
mom_hs == 1 & mom_work > 2 ~ "High",
),
# Create age groups
age_group = case_when(
mom_age >= 17 & mom_age <= 20 ~ "Ages 17-20",
mom_age >= 21 & mom_age <= 23 ~ "Ages 21-23",
mom_age >= 24 & mom_age <= 26 ~ "Ages 24-26",
mom_age >= 27 & mom_age <= 29 ~ "Ages 27-29"
),
# Create IQ terciles for grouping
iq_group = case_when(
mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.33, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Lower IQ",
mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.67, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Middle IQ",
TRUE ~ "Higher IQ"
)
)

kidiq$age_group <- factor(kidiq$age_group, labels = c(
"Ages 17-20","Ages 21-23", "Ages 24-26","Ages 27-29"))
kidiq$iq_group <- factor(kidiq$iq_group, labels = c(
"Lower IQ", "Middle IQ", "Higher IQ"))
kidiq$work_status <- factor(kidiq$work_status, labels = c(
"Not working", "Part-time", "Full-time","Full-time+"))
kidiq$family_advantage <- factor(kidiq$family_advantage, labels = c(
"Low", "Mixed", "High"))
kidiq <- as.data.frame(kidiq)


To indicate different effects on IQ, I added additional dimensions using different colors, size, and faceting to differentiate. In the end, I was able to tell a story about social mobility and opportunity through a readable violin plot.


k1 <- ggplot(kidiq, aes(x = family_advantage, y = kid_score, color = age_group)) +
geom_violin() +
facet_wrap(~age_group) +
scale_color_brewer(palette = "RdPu") +
labs(
title = "Family Ties? Does a mother’s educational and employment
background affect their child's performance",
subtitle = "Correlation between family advantage with child's",
x = "Mother's Household Advantage",
y = "Child's Test Score",
caption = "Data: Test scores and mother's characteristics") +
theme_minimal()
print(k1)



The correlation between a mother’s educational and employment background, collectively known as Family Advantage, and the academic performance of their children is shown across several age groups. Most data seems to be sporadic,with notable exceptions being unemployed and full-time working mothers in the age range 24-26, and unemployed mothers in their late teens, having children who reached the mode performance scores.

By: Akmal G on November 4th, 2025
For this project, I created a visualization that shows how electoral turnouts differ between the UK, Scotland, Ireland and Wales, from a very complicated dataset.
Step 1 - Load Packages
Firstly, I download several packages. Installing the “stringr” package allows for manipulate characters, use whitespace, and match patterns between function. I also install the “readr” package that allows us to read rectangular data (i.e. CSV and TSV) from delimited files, and the “ggplot2” package allows us to produce statistical data and graphics.
THere are also additional packages I need to doanload for readibility; the “curl” package provides bindings to the libcurl C library, while “tidyverse” package allows our data and graphs to be presented in a more presentable fashion.


library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(curl)


Step 2 - Raw data filtration
First, I place the election result data from the website into object uk_csv. I place the read data from the website and removing column names from the previous object into a new object, uk_raw.I then replace all unreadable data with \s+ with readable underscores, I recheck all data using ‘print’ before moving on.


uk_csv <- "https://electionresults.parliament.uk/general-elections/6/candidacies.csv"
uk_raw <- readr::read_csv(uk_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
names(uk_raw) <- names(uk_raw) %>% tolower() %>% str_replace_all("\\s+", "_")

For the 25 highest-turnout places, with a larger range of data, the average voter turnout is around 70 to 75%.

Step 6 - Investigate Turnout
We now print out the turnoutrat by Constituent Countries of the UK. ‘n’ indicates the number of sample constituencies from each country (e.g. there are 543 sample constituncies from England). It is important to know the number of samples in a country to ensure the workings behind the mean and median turnout. I then create country summary (mean, median, n), ordered by mean turnout, and compile it into an object.


turnout_by_country <- uk %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_turnout   = mean(turnout_registered, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_turnout = median(turnout_registered, na.rm = TRUE),
    n              = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_turnout))
print(turnout_by_country)

1 England                  60.1           60.7   543
2 Scotland                 59.2           58.6    57
3 Northern Ireland         57.1           58.2    18
4 Wales                    56.2           56.8    32

Step 7 - Visualisation of Findings
Using ggplot, I finally visualize the findings on turnout on each country. England shows the highest median turnout. One plausible reason for this is its large sample size of 543 constituencies …and hence a greater chance of finding a high turnout rate.
I added three changes to the visualization in order to improve it. I changed the bar width from 0.7 to 0.95, to improve visibility of the compatibility between the countries’ turnout. I changed the expansion multiplier from c(0, 0.05) to c(-0.5, -0.35), I added geom_text to add the turnout (y-value) of each country, so it magnifies the margin of difference between the turnout percentage between the y values of 50 and 65.
There were two failed approaches. I tried to change the geom_col into geom_line and geom_bar, but neither were interesting enough to look at. I tried to change the geom_col into geom_point, but there was not enough data and looked too simple. And stupid.
Improved Framework


ggplot(turnout_by_country, aes(country, mean_turnout, colours)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.95, fill = "#59c7d4") +  # bar = mean turnout
  geom_text(aes(label = signif(mean_turnout, digits = 3)), 
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), 
            vjust = -0.75, color = "black", size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(-0.5, -0.35))) +
  labs(
    title = "UK 2024 General Election: Mean Turnout by Country",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Turnout (% of registered voters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

articles.title: Sentiment Analysis of FOMC Bank Statements
articles.contents:
By: Akmal G on March 26th, 2026
In this project, I looked at the use of uncertainty language as well as output and inflation topics in a subsection of Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) statements made by the U.S. central bank. At the end, I also create an additional investigation on the role of energy in the wording of these statements and its confidence.
Applying dictionaries to FOMC policy statements
Because the file names actually have the date of the meeting, we are going to collect the filenames in an object.


library(quanteda)
library(readtext)
require(ggplot2)
filenames <- list.files("FOMC", "\\.txt$") # Import data


Extracting FOMCs from a list of files, I then read these texts using str.
I then turn their texts into a corpus.


txts <-  readtext(paste0("FOMC",  "/", "*.txt"))[]
str(txts)

Accuracy asks what percentage of all the observations our system labeled correctly. Although accuracy might seem a natural metric, we generally don’t use it for text classification tasks. That’s because accuracy doesn’t work well when the classes are unbalanced. Our data wasn’t so imbalanced so thats something to think about.
That’s why instead of accuracy we generally turn to two other metrics: precision and recall. Precision measures the percentage of the items that the system detected (i.e., the system labeled as positive) that are in fact positive (i.eare positive according to the human gold labels). Recall measures the percentage of items actually present in the input that were correctly identified by the system
